issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: 'Reminders of victims' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver, where the patient is the victim rather than someone exposed to other victims. This trigger implies a different trauma context unless there is additional unreported trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is difficult to fit with the available profile for a 23-year-old single ship captain with childhood caregiver abuse, because no salient caregiving/protective role failure is otherwise represented in the triggers, threat, or memory content. It reads as a role-specific trauma appraisal from a different context rather than a coherent extension of the rest of this profile.

vignette:
Mai, at twenty-three, is one of the youngest captains in her shipping line, a position she earned through a fierce and solitary focus. The open ocean had always felt like the only place vast enough to escape the memories that crowded her on land. The trauma began long before she ever saw the sea, in the small, dark rooms of her childhood home. For years, her uncle, her primary caregiver, used the night as his shield. The abuse was often preceded by long, silent car rides where the click of the door locks echoed the feeling of being utterly trapped. He was the only consistent male figure in her young life, and his presence became synonymous with a suffocating dread. She learned early that safety was an illusion and that the world was a fundamentally dangerous place.

Now, years later, the past ambushes her in the very place she sought refuge. Any time she is alone with one of her male crewmates in a passageway or on the bridge, the trigger is pulled. The same happens when she has to ride in a vehicle with others during shore leave, a rare event she avoids at all costs. These moments instantly ignite a profound sense of threat. Her entire body clenches, a constant, humming tension that prepares her for a danger only she can see. A wave of raw fear, thick and suffocating, rises in her chest, and her mind immediately begins plotting exits. She finds herself mentally mapping the quickest path to the open deck or the nearest emergency hatch, a silent, frantic calculation she performs before she can feel even a moment's ease in any enclosed space.

These triggered states do more than just flood her with fear; they confirm the darkest beliefs she holds about herself and the world. When a simple car ride with her crew to pick up supplies leaves her trembling and nauseous, it serves as visceral proof that the world is, and always will be, a place of hidden threats. Watching her crewmates laugh and talk, oblivious to her internal terror, deepens her conviction that she is irrevocably set apart from others. This profound sense of isolation feeds a deeper, more painful appraisal: that there must be something fundamentally wrong with her. She sees her reactions not as a legacy of her past, but as evidence of a personal defect, a brokenness that makes her unworthy of the connection and ease she sees in everyone else.

This cycle of belief and fear has become self-perpetuating. Because Mai is so certain that she is defective and that the world is a dangerous place, she is relentlessly vigilant. Her mind actively scans for the very things that terrify her, making her hyper-aware of any potential trigger. The approach of nightfall is not just a change in the watch schedule; it is the arrival of the time she is most vulnerable. A male crew member's presence is not a neutral event but an immediate potential threat that her body registers long before her conscious mind does. This constant state of alert, her body already tense and primed for danger, means that when a trigger does appear, her reaction is immediate and overwhelming. The fear and the vigilance feed one another, ensuring that she is always either anticipating a threat or actively experiencing one.

Her life has narrowed to the confines of this cycle. As captain, she can't avoid her crew, so she has developed rigid rules: all meetings happen on the open bridge, never in her small office. She takes the midnight watch herself, forcing herself to stay awake through the darkest hours under the bright fluorescent lights, terrified of waking up disoriented in her pitch-black cabin. Her crew respects her but sees her as distant, cold, and strange, which only reinforces her feeling of being an outsider. The isolation she feels is no longer just a belief; it is a reality she has constructed. She came to therapy after a storm last month when a power failure plunged the ship into darkness. Her panicked, frozen response nearly led to a critical error, a moment that made her realize her carefully managed world was threatening to destroy the one thing that had ever made her feel capable: her career. She is terrified of losing her ship, but even more terrified that she will never feel safe in her own skin.
